content:
# Sirach 30 — Disagreement Log
**Chapter:** Sirach 30 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 14

---

## Disagreement 001 — 30:1 "continue-to-chastise / keep on chastising / discipline consistently"
**Verse:** 30:1
**EMET:** "will-continue-to-chastise him"
**LOGOS:** "will keep on chastising him"
**PNEUMA:** "will discipline him consistently"
**Issue:** παιδεύσει — "will discipline/educate/chastise." The verb implies corporal correction in this context. "Keep on chastising" (LOGOS) captures the iterative sense of the imperfective. "Discipline consistently" (PNEUMA) is interpretively neutral. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "will keep on chastising him."

---

## Disagreement 002 — 30:2 "be-benefited / profit from him"
**Verse:** 30:2
**EMET:** "will-be-benefited by-him"
**LOGOS:** "will profit from him"
**PNEUMA:** "he'll be worth something to you"
**Issue:** ὀνήσεται — "will be benefited/profit." LOGOS and PNEUMA are both accurate. "Profit" has commercial connotations; "benefit" is more neutral. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "will profit from him."

---

## Disagreement 003 — 30:3 "provoke-jealousy / make envious"
**Verse:** 30:3
**EMET:** "will-provoke-jealousy in-his-enemy"
**LOGOS:** "will make his enemy envious"
**PNEUMA:** "you'll make your enemies jealous"
**Issue:** ζηλώσει ἐχθρούς — "will make enemies envious." All agree on meaning. Minor wording differences. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "will make his enemy envious."

---

## Disagreement 004 — 30:7 "coddles / over-pampers" and binding wounds
**Verse:** 30:7
**EMET:** "He-who-coddles his-son will-bind-up his-wounds"
**LOGOS:** "He who coddles his son will bind up his wounds"
**PNEUMA:** "Coddle your son and you'll be wrapping his wounds later"
**Issue:** ψηλαφᾷ — "strokes/handles gently/coddles." The irony is that the over-indulgent parent ends up treating the son's self-inflicted wounds. PNEUMA's "later" is added for clarity. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "He who coddles his son will bind up his wounds."

---

## Disagreement 005 — 30:8 "unbroken-horse / horse that's never been broken"
**Verse:** 30:8
**EMET:** "An-unbroken-horse becomes-stubborn"
**LOGOS:** "An unbroken horse turns stubborn"
**PNEUMA:** "A horse that's never been broken becomes unmanageable"
**Issue:** ἵππος ἀδαμάσευτος — "an unbroken/untamed horse." PNEUMA adds "unmanageable" — a stronger descriptor. "Stubborn" is closer to the Greek σκληρός ("hard/stubborn/stiff-necked"). SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "An unbroken horse turns stubborn."

---

## Disagreement 006 — 30:12 "bow-down his-neck / bend his neck"
**Verse:** 30:12
**EMET:** "Bow-down his-neck in-his-youth"
**LOGOS:** "Bow down his neck in his youth"
**PNEUMA:** "Bend his neck while he's young"
**Issue:** κάμψον τὸν τράχηλον αὐτοῦ — "bend his neck." All agree; PNEUMA's "while he's young" is a paraphrase of "in his youth." SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "Bow down his neck in his youth."

---

## Disagreement 007 — 30:14 "healthy and-strong / healthy and strong in body"
**Verse:** 30:14
**EMET:** "who-is-healthy and-strong in-his-body"
**LOGOS:** "who is healthy and strong in body"
**PNEUMA:** "who is fit and strong"
**Issue:** ὑγιαίνων καὶ εὔτονος — "healthy and strong/vigorous." PNEUMA's "fit" is modern fitness language. "Strong in body" is more precise. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "who is healthy and strong in body."

---

## Disagreement 008 — 30:15 "wholeness / soundness / sound body"
**Verse:** 30:15
**EMET:** "Health and wholeness are-better-than all-gold"
**LOGOS:** "Health and soundness of body are better than all gold"
**PNEUMA:** "Good health, a sound body"
**Issue:** ὑγιεία καὶ εὐεξία — "health and good condition/soundness." EMET uses "wholeness" which is the more literal rendering of εὐεξία (eu-hexia = good having/condition). "Soundness" (LOGOS) is more idiomatic. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "Health and soundness of body are better than all gold."

---

## Disagreement 009 — 30:17 "eternal-rest / endless sleep / eternal rest"
**Verse:** 30:17
**EMET:** "an-eternal-rest than a-chronic-illness"
**LOGOS:** "eternal rest better than chronic illness"
**PNEUMA:** "endless sleep is better than never-ending illness"
**Issue:** ἀνάπαυσις αἰώνιος — "eternal rest." PNEUMA's "endless sleep" substitutes "sleep" for "rest" — which loses the eschatological connotation of ἀνάπαυσις (a term used for the rest of the dead). SOPHIA follows LOGOS/EMET.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "eternal rest better than chronic illness."

---

## Disagreement 010 — 30:18 "offerings placed before a tomb"
**Verse:** 30:18
**EMET:** "like-offerings placed before a-tomb"
**LOGOS:** "like offerings placed in front of a tomb"
**PNEUMA:** "like offerings laid before a tomb"
**Issue:** θυσίας ἐπικειμένης τάφῳ — "offerings placed at/upon a tomb." The image is of tomb-cult food offerings that the dead cannot use. All agents agree. Minor wording differences only.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "like offerings placed before a tomb."

---

## Disagreement 011 — 30:19-20 idol/eunuch comparison — its structure
**Verses:** 30:19-20
**EMET:** Treats vv. 19-20 as a continuous sentence
**LOGOS:** Same
**PNEUMA:** Same but with interpretive additions
**Issue:** The verse structure is: "What does an idol offering profit? (For it cannot eat or smell.) So too the one punished by the LORD — seeing with eyes and groaning, like a eunuch embracing a virgin and sighing." PNEUMA's "someone the LORD has brought low" for "punished by the LORD" — κολαζόμενος ὑπὸ κυρίου — is interpretive. "Punished" is more precise than "brought low."
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "So too the one who is afflicted by the LORD" — "afflicted" as a middle ground between "punished" and "brought low."

---

## Disagreement 012 — 30:22 "Joy-of-heart is-the-life / Gladness of heart"
**Verse:** 30:22
**EMET:** "Joy-of-heart is-the-life of a-man"
**LOGOS:** "Gladness of heart is a man's life"
**PNEUMA:** "A happy heart is life itself"
**Issue:** εὐφροσύνη καρδίας — "gladness/joy of heart." PNEUMA's "A happy heart" renders the construct idiomatically. LOGOS's "gladness of heart" preserves the construct noun. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "Gladness of heart is a man's life."

---

## Disagreement 013 — 30:23 "Deceive yourself / Console yourself / Cheer yourself up"
**Verse:** 30:23
**EMET:** "Deceive yourself and console your-soul"
**LOGOS:** "Console yourself and give your heart cheer"
**PNEUMA:** "Cheer yourself up, comfort your heart"
**Issue:** παραλόγισαι σεαυτόν — "mislead/deceive yourself." EMET preserves the startling imperative: literally "deceive yourself!" LOGOS and PNEUMA soften to "console" and "cheer." The Greek instruction to self-deception (in service of comfort against despair) is remarkable and should be preserved.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "Console yourself and cheer your heart" — "console" softens but the note on παραλόγισαι is preserved in the log.

---

## Disagreement 014 — 30:24 "Jealousy and anger / Envy and anger"
**Verse:** 30:24
**EMET:** "Jealousy and anger shorten-life"
**LOGOS:** "Envy and anger shorten life"
**PNEUMA:** "Envy and anger cut years off your life"
**Issue:** ζῆλος καὶ θυμός — "jealousy/zeal and anger." ζῆλος can mean either "zeal" (positive) or "jealousy/envy" (negative). In this context "envy/jealousy" is clearly intended. LOGOS and PNEUMA's "envy" is accurate. SOPHIA follows LOGOS.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA: "Envy and anger shorten life."
